subtitle: A guide to the early Network Working Group notes and their status in February 1971.

tldr.problem: The NWG/RFC series had reached 102 notes, making it difficult to see which documents were current, obsolete, or superseded and what topics remained open.
tldr.mechanism: P. Karp organizes the notes into nine categories with subcategories, summarizes documents, and lists a smaller set that reflects the current status of topics.
tldr.outcome: This initial guide was issued as an NWG/RFC for comments for approximately two weeks. The text says an official version was planned for March 26 as a separate series.

today: The unit metadata lists RFC 100's status as Unknown and no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. The memo is a February 1971 snapshot and says that an official separate guide was planned for March 26.

sections.title: Why the Guide Was Written
sections.content:
The NWG/RFC series had reached 102 notes by February 1971. This guide aims to organize them, identify topics under discussion, point to relevant notes, and indicate whether each note is current, obsolete, or superseded.

The guide identifies a smaller subset of notes that the author considered useful for quickly learning the current status of topics. It also summarizes notes for readers who want to follow how a topic developed. The author asks for comments for approximately two weeks and says an official version is planned for March 26 as a separate document series.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide helps readers sort the NWG/RFC notes by topic and status. It includes both a short list for quick orientation and summaries for readers who want more history.

sections.title: The Nine Topic Categories
sections.content:
The guide divides notes into nine lettered categories, A through I: Administrative; Host/IMP Protocol; Host/Host Protocol; Subsystem Level Protocol; Measurement on Network; Network Experience; Site Documentation; Accounting; and Other. Categories are divided into subcategories, and the guide identifies official documents, unresolved issues, and planned documents where applicable.

For example, the Host/Host category covers establishing and ending connections, flow control, error control, interrupts, and links. The subsystem-level category covers user-facing topics such as logger, console, Telnet, data transformation, graphics, and file transmission; the guide says there is no official document for that category and that its issues remain unresolved.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide groups notes into nine broad topics, from protocol specifications to network experience and accounting. It also points out where decisions remain open.

sections.title: The Current-Status List and Index
sections.content:
The guide provides a list of NWG/RFC numbers that, in February 1971, it considered to reflect current status. It then organizes that subset by category and subcategory. The guide notes that much of the current subset concerns subsystem-level protocol topics, where many issues were unresolved.

The final portion lists the notes numbered 1 through 102 with their titles, authors, dates, and category references. This lets readers find a note by number and see which topic area it belongs to.
sections.plainLanguage: The guide identifies the notes it considered current at the time and links each note to a topic. Its numbered index helps readers look up an individual document.
